claims.text: The baseline material is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic disordered high-entropy alloy.
The baseline alloy contains inherent compositional and local lattice distortions.
Changing the concentration of a transition metal with substantial atomic-size mismatch will systematically alter local lattice distortion while retaining a high-entropy alloy state.
Local lattice distortions enhance magnetoelastic coupling in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced magnetoelastic coupling lowers the energy barrier for magnetic ordering transitions at low applied fields.
Controlled local lattice strains create regions with enhanced magnetic exchange interactions.
The enhanced magnetic exchange interactions couple strongly to selected lattice vibrations.
The proposed strain-mediated magnetoelastic coupling enables a large magnetocaloric effect at low applied magnetic fields.
The distributed local distortions promote rapid heat exchange.
The distributed local distortions minimize thermal hysteresis.
The proposed distortion distribution supports long-term mechanical integrity.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will exhibit a stronger magnetocaloric effect at lower applied fields.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will exhibit reduced thermal hysteresis during cyclic operation.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will have similar or improved heat-transfer performance.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy will have similar or improved mechanical performance.
The hypothesis is expected to apply only while the modified compositions retain the high-entropy, disordered crystal state.
The hypothesis is expected to apply from room temperature to moderately elevated magnetic-refrigeration operating temperatures.
Large compositional variations that disrupt the disordered crystal structure lie outside the proposed regime.
Unintended phase separation or secondary-phase formation could complicate interpretation of the intervention.
